newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain seen among first EMU members in 1999 - poll.
newsitem.headline: Spain seen among first EMU members in 1999 - poll.

text.p: A majority of economists polled by Reuters think Spain's 1997 budget is realistic and will help it be among the first members of a European single currency.
Twelve of the 16 questioned on Monday and Tuesday said they expected growth to meet the official target of three percent next year.
Some cautioned that the forecast may be optimistic and said their own forecasts for gross domestic product (GDP) growth were slightly lower.
The main obstacle to Spanish growth could, ironically, be stagnation in other European countries, several economists pointed out.

Nine of them expect Spain to be among the first members of a European economic and monetary union (EMU) at the start in January 1999. Some of those who don't expect Spain to make the first wave of members say it will join within two years.

Among the Maastricht criteria which countries must meet to join the EMU, inflation was considered the hardest since it escapes direct government control. Seven contributors said the budget deficit would also be a major obstacle to overcome.
Objectively seen, the debt to GDP criteria was the toughest to meet, but most of those polled expected this requirement to be flexible.

A majority expected the Bank of Spain to lower its key money market rate by another quarter-point from 6.75 percent before the end of the year. All but one expected the rate to fall in 1997 to between 6.00 and 6.25 percent.

The peseta is seen oscillating in a narrow band of 84.00 to 85.00 against the German mark until the end of 1996, with most economists expecting support to hold at 84.30. It will trade between 83.00 and 86.00 in 1997, they predicted.
Those surveyed saw the spread between 10-year Spanish bonos and their German counterparts hovering around 170 basis points until the end of the year.
However, a sharp rise in bonds on Wednesday brought the spread down to 157 basis points, a level some economists had predicted for 1997.
Few economists made forecasts for the Madrid bourse, but those that did saw the Ibex-35 index rising towards 4,500 by the end of 1996 and 5,100 in 1997.
